What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Run and observe the baseline calculator
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run the provided calculator.c to see variables, scanf, and arithmetic outputs.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand how variables are declared, how scanf uses &, and how printf format specifiers map to types.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We'll compile and run the calculator.c file. Watch each prompt and match it to the scanf and printf lines in code. Notice the ampersand before variables in scanf — that's giving scanf the address-of the variable so it can store input. Predict the outputs for inputs ten and three before running.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Input: 10 and 3. Expected outputs: Sum: 13, Difference: 7, Product: 30, Quotient: 3.33.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You are building a command-line tool that performs quick arithmetic for small tasks and needs to interact with the user.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run: clang calculator.c -o calculator && echo -e "10\n3\n" | ./calculator. Say aloud which lines printed Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient and point to their code lines.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting the ampersand in scanf will likely cause a runtime error because scanf needs a memory address to store the input.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You ran the program and matched output to code: declarations, scanf with &, and printf with correct format specifiers.
codeSteps: Open calculator.c and read through lines. Identify variable declarations at the top.
Find the two scanf lines and note the ampersand.
Compile and run using the provided command and observe output.

teachingPlaylist.title: Modify one line to see integer division
teachingPlaylist.description: Change the quotient printing line to use integer division and observe truncation of fractional part.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Experience the difference between integer and floating-point division and why type casting matters.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Edit the printf that prints the quotient: replace the floating-point format and cast with an integer format and expression. Recompile and rerun. Compare outputs and explain why the fractional part disappeared.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Change to: printf("Quotient: %i\n", num1 / num2);. With 10 and 3 the printed quotient will be 3.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You're debugging a calculation that now prints unexpected whole numbers instead of decimals.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Make the small edit, compile, and run with 10 and 3. Observe quotient becomes an integer.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Changing the format to %i while passing a float expression will lead to undefined prints; ensure expression result type matches format specifier.
teachingPlaylist.recap: A single-line change showed how C chooses division semantics based on operand types.
codeSteps: Locate the printf that prints the quotient.
Replace it with printf("Quotient: %i\n", num1 / num2);
Compile and run to observe integer division.

teachingPlaylist.title: Add remainder and average calculations
teachingPlaylist.description: Extend the program to compute the remainder with % and a floating-point average.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Practice integrating new arithmetic operators and ensure correct format specifiers and casting for results.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Insert two print statements: one for the remainder using the modulo operator, and one for the average ensuring floating-point division. Choose formats %i for integers and %.2f for float outputs.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Add printf("Remainder: %i\n", num1 % num2); and printf("Average: %.2f\n", (float)(num1 + num2) / 2); then run with 10 and 3 to see Remainder: 1 and Average: 6.50.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You need to show more helpful results from a calculator to the user without changing the input method.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Insert the two lines after product, compile, and run examples including 5 and 2 and 10 and 3.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to cast before division when computing average will produce integer average and lose decimals.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You added functionality that combined modulo and float casting, producing new useful outputs.
codeSteps: After printing product, add a printf for remainder using num1 % num2.
Add a printf for Average using (float)(num1 + num2) / 2 and format %.2f.
Compile and test with several input pairs.

teachingPlaylist.title: Handle division by zero and verify robustness
teachingPlaylist.description: Add an if-statement to prevent division or modulo by zero and test edge cases.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Learn defensive programming: check input before operations that require non-zero denominators.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Wrap the quotient and remainder prints inside an if that tests whether num two equals zero. If zero, print a friendly message and skip the dangerous operations. Recompile and test with a second input of zero to confirm your guard works.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample:
Add: if (num2 == 0) { printf("Cannot divide by zero.
"); } else { printf("Remainder: %i
", num1 % num2); printf("Quotient: %.2f
", (float)num1 / num2); }
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Your calculator will be used by other people who may type zero; it must not crash their terminal session.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Implement the guard, compile, then run with inputs 8 and 0 and observe that the program prints a warning instead of crashing.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Adding the guard but still performing modulo before the check will not prevent the crash—order matters.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You made the program robust by checking input before sensitive operations and tested the edge case where the second number is zero.
codeSteps: Remove any direct quotient/remainder prints and replace them with an if (num2 == 0) guard.
Inside the else branch, print remainder and floating-point quotient.
Compile and test with zero and non-zero values for num2.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the baseline calculator
tasks.narratorGuide: Goal: run the provided calculator.c to observe variables, scanf, and arithmetic. First principle: a variable is a named memory box; int stores whole numbers. Model: compile with clang and run, type two integers when prompted. While running, watch the prompts, then the four outputs: Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient. Prediction: with inputs ten and three, expect Sum: 13, Difference: 7, Product: 30, and Quotient approximately 3.33. Connect: notice the ampersand in scanf — that's the address-of operator telling scanf where to store input. Pause: after running, say aloud what each printed line corresponds to in the code. Good observation.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: See integer division by changing one line
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: Name the goal — show integer division. OBSERVE: Look at the line that prints the quotient. CHANGE: Edit that single line to remove the cast and use %i and num1 / num2. TEST: Recompile and run with 10 and 3. EXPECT: Quotient will print 3, not 3.33. EXPLAIN: Why? Both operands are ints; integer division discards the fraction. EXTEND: Try other pairs like 5 and 2 and predict the output before running.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Add remainder and average
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: We're adding new outputs that are common in calculators. OBSERVE: Identify where product is printed. CHANGE: Insert two lines: printf("Remainder: %i\n", num1 % num2); and printf("Average: %.2f\n", (float)(num1 + num2) / 2); TEST: Recompile and run with 10 and 3. EXPECT: Remainder: 1 and Average: 6.50. EXPLAIN: The modulo operator % produces the remainder. Casting ensures the average shows decimals. EXTEND: Try negative numbers or larger values.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Handle division by zero safely
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: Why check for zero? Because modulo and division by zero are undefined. OBSERVE: Find where quotient and remainder are printed. CHANGE: Replace those prints with an if (num2 == 0) guard that prints "Cannot divide by zero." else prints remainder and quotient (using a cast for float quotient). TEST: Recompile and run with second input zero. EXPECT: The program should still print sum, difference, product and then the cannot-divide message, and not crash. EXPLAIN: This simple guard prevents undefined behavior and makes your program robust.
